The Problem
Same restaurant, three different review experiences · iOS · Android · Desktop
Reviews existed —
but they weren't doing any convincing.

Diners had reviews available, but the experience was fragmented across platforms and buried the one line that actually sways a decision — a standout quote, a simple "would you come back?" signal — under generic star breakdowns and long text blocks.

Cross-platform inconsistencies
iOS, Android and Desktop showed different visuals, navigation and even different rating scales for the same restaurant — the community score wasn't reading as one trustworthy number.
Not enough useful information
The restaurant profile surfaced a single review. With very little context about the rating itself, diners had no fast way to judge if a place was actually right for them.
Accessibility issues
Low contrast, small tap targets and inconsistent hierarchy across the reviews section made it harder to use for a meaningful share of diners.
Inconsistent UX writing
The product spoke differently to its cross-platform users — labels, tone and structure shifted from screen to screen, weakening the sense of one coherent product.
Research & Learnings
Reviews are read before the decision — and today, over half of diners don't trust what they find.

Research takeaway
Diners don't want more reviews. They want the one that tells them what they need to know — fast.
Beyond the score, many users specifically look for photos shared by other customers before they trust a restaurant's reputation.
Reviews Mission · What I do
Reviews are crucial in making a decision.

Food, value for money, service and noise all determine whether a place is perfect and meets the user's expectations.

Regarding the restaurants, the reviews improve their rating following the highest standards of service, food and atmosphere — so the module has to work for diners deciding where to eat, and for restaurants building their reputation.

Design Exploration · Two directions
Vertical scroll or carousel — I prototyped both before betting on one.

Two proposals came out of the wireframing stage: a vertical-scroll summary that reads top to bottom like a feed, and a horizontal carousel that lets diners swipe through the highlighted quote, the would-return stat and individual reviews as separate cards. Both kept the same information architecture — the difference was how much diners had to scroll versus swipe to get through it.

Highlighted quote
The single most compelling line from real reviews, surfaced above the fold.
"Would return" stat
A simple, structured trust signal instead of raw star math.
Structured review cards
Reviewer, score, date and photos in one scannable, consistent format.
One system, three platforms
Same rating scale, same components and same UX writing on iOS, Android and Web.
01 · Vertical version — full summary, rating breakdown, sorted reviews
02 · Carousel version — swipeable cards, frequency-word filters, ratings modal
Outcome · A/B test results
The carousel version won.

Both directions shipped as an A/B test against the old reviews module. The carousel version — leading with the highlighted quote and the would-return stat, then letting diners swipe through the rest — outperformed on both the engagement and the business metric, confirming the original research: diners don't need more reviews, they need the right one, fast.
